consensus_summary: The blind consensus treats kaph, when read symbolically, as centering on God's intimate, permanent care and remembrance of His people, anchored in Isaiah 49:16 (engraving on the palms), often extended devotionally to Christ's nail-pierced hands. Secondary recognized senses include spread/lifted palms in prayer, clean palms as moral innocence, divine power and sovereign measurement (Isaiah 40:12), and human agency/deeds. One response (C) denies any settled symbolic consensus, and several note that power/agency symbolism attaches to hand-terms generally, sometimes yad rather than kaph.
book_summary: The book defines kaph as 'the open hand' — the hand laid open to cover (Exodus 33:22; Psalm 139:5), carry (Isaiah 49:16), and offer (Proverbs 31:20; prayer spread toward heaven) — and explicitly separates it from yad, 'the hand of power,' citing Isaiah 62:3 as holding both terms in one verse. It thus unifies covering, carrying, giving, and prayer under one lexical-symbolic core of openness, while assigning power to a different Hebrew word.
consensus_core_identification: Kaph symbolizes God's intimate covenant care and unforgettable remembrance of His people (Isaiah 49:16), with prayer, purity of deeds, and divine power/agency as recognized secondary senses.
book_core_identification: Kaph is the open hand — covering, carrying, offering — deliberately distinguished from yad, the hand of power; its symbolism is openness (protection, bearing, giving, prayer), not power.
boundary_disagreement: The book broadens the core beyond the consensus's dominant Isaiah 49:16 remembrance motif to a unified 'open hand' concept that treats covering (Ex 33:22; Ps 139:5), carrying/engraving (Isa 49:16), offering to the poor (Prov 31:20), and spread palms in prayer as one integrated sense. Simultaneously it excludes and reclassifies the power/agency/sovereign-control sense (which Responses B and D admit for kaph, e.g., Isaiah 40:12) as belonging to yad, not kaph. Consensus alternatives such as clapping, clean palms/deeds, and sole-of-foot possession are silently dropped.
material_contradiction: None at the level of central referent. The book's protective-care and prayer readings sit inside the consensus cluster; the disagreement is a boundary claim (kaph ≠ hand of power) rather than a replacement of the consensus identification. Response C's power alternative already flags that power symbolism often rests on yad, anticipating the book's distinction.
rationale: The book preserves the consensus's recognizable referent — the palm as the locus of God's protective care and remembrance and of human prayer and giving — so this is not DIVERGENT or NOVEL. But it materially restructures the category: instead of a dominant remembrance symbol with assorted secondary senses, it posits a single lexical-symbolic core (openness: cover, carry, offer) and draws a hard boundary against the power symbolism that two consensus responses include for kaph, assigning it to yad. That is a real change of extension and precision within the same category, which fits REFINED with BOOK_BROADENS at the core (a wider unified sense than the consensus primary) and PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION at the extension (power cases moved out; prayer and giving moved from alternatives into the core).
strongest_objection: One could argue MATCH: every element the book names (covering, engraving, giving to the poor, spread palms in prayer) appears somewhere in the consensus responses, and Response C even anticipates the kaph/yad distinction, so the book might be seen as merely reorganizing agreed material rather than changing its extension. The reply is that the book's exclusion of power from kaph's meaning and its elevation of a unified 'openness' core over the consensus's dominant remembrance motif is a substantive boundary claim, not mere wording — Responses B and D would have to retract kaph-as-power readings of texts like Isaiah 40:12.
